paras: The attempted lynching at Jacksonville, Alabama, was an August 1890 effort by a mob of about 1,000 people to seize and hang an unnamed Black man held by the sheriff in Calhoun County, who was accused of having tried to rape the young daughter of a white man, Benjamin Carpenter. The sheriff moved the prisoner first to Anniston and then farther south, while the mob followed, chartered a special train and cut the wires. Wire reports predicted a "first-class hanging," but no confirmation that the man was killed appears in the coverage, and a brief Texas report that he had been lynched appears to compress the same dispatch.

A dispatch from Montgomery dated August 16, 1890, reported that about four weeks earlier a Black man had tried to rape a young white girl, the daughter of Benjamin Carpenter, at Jacksonville in Calhoun County. The man was arrested, and for two nights the jail was guarded. None of the reports named the accused man or the girl, and versions relayed through New Orleans gave her father's name as "Ben Carter" and the town as "Jackson."

On the night of Thursday, August 14, a mob of about 1,000 set out for the jail, "swearing they would have the negro or burn the jail." The sheriff, in the dispatch's words, "was too quick for them" and sent the prisoner to Anniston. The next day the mob reorganized at Anniston, "swearing vengeance on the negro," and the sheriff again moved his prisoner, this time to an unnamed point to the south, "presumably Talladega."

Late that afternoon the mob chartered a special train and cut the wires. The Washington Evening Star's version ended by predicting that the mob "will probably have a first-class hanging tonight," while the New-York Tribune, crediting the New Orleans Picayune, wrote that "it is supposed" the hanging took place before morning.
No later report of the prisoner's fate, of where he was finally taken, or of any inquest, arrests or official response appears in the coverage.

The episode reached readers almost entirely through one Montgomery dispatch, which the Washington Evening Star, the Alexandria Gazette and the New York Sun printed on August 16 and 17. The Wheeling Sunday Register and the Indianapolis Journal carried it on August 17. Weeklies at Watertown and Eagle River, Wisconsin, reprinted it on August 20 and 23.

The wording of the charge shifted from paper to paper: the Star and the Tribune said the man "tried to rape" the girl, the Alexandria Gazette said he "tried to assault" her, and the Wisconsin reprints said flatly that he "assaulted" her. Headlines ranged from the Star's "Lynchers on a Special Train" and the Tribune's "Chasing a Negro with a Special Train" to the Wheeling paper's "First Class Hanging" over "An Alabama Mob Thirsting for a Negro's Blood." The Wisconsin weeklies called the accused "the Brute" and a "Negro Ravisher," while the Indianapolis Journal ran the same text under the headline "Southerners at Their Favorite Sport." No account of the episode in the Black press appears in the coverage.

A two-sentence item in the San Antonio Daily Light, datelined New Orleans, said that a mob of 1,000 "took a negro from jail last night and lynched him" at "Jackson, Calhoun county." The Fort Worth Daily Gazette printed the same New Orleans special at length, with the same "Ben Carter" and "Jackson" spellings, and said only that the mob "will probably have a first-class hanging before noon." The San Antonio item therefore appears to turn a prediction into a report of a completed lynching, since every fuller version of the dispatch, including the Tribune's, describes a pursuit whose outcome was not yet known.

A mob of 1,000 sought to hang a man accused of attempted rape (A1, A4), but the fuller dispatches report only an expected hanging (A1, A4, A8); the lone report of a completed lynching (A3) appears to condense the same New Orleans special that, printed in full, predicted rather than reported a hanging (A8).

Every account traces to one Montgomery dispatch, relayed through New Orleans (A1, A4, A8); the San Antonio report of a lynching (A3) is a shortened version of that same special, not an independent report.

The Wheeling Sunday Register headlined 'First Class Hanging' and 'An Alabama Mob Thirsting for a Negro's Blood'.
Wisconsin reprints called the accused 'the Brute' and a 'Negro Ravisher' and changed 'tried to rape' to 'assaulted'.
The Indianapolis Journal headlined the dispatch 'Southerners at Their Favorite Sport'.
